questions.q: Which observability pillar shows where in a multi-service request the time is spent?

options.why: Correct. Traces show the sequence and timing of operations across services.
Metrics show that something changed, in aggregate.
Alerts aren't one of the three pillars.
Logs explain why a specific operation behaved as it did.

questions.hint: Metrics show trends and logs show detail. The pillar that follows one request across services is the third one.
questions.explain: Metrics: something changed. Traces: where. Logs: why.

questions.q: Which standard does OpenTelemetry use to propagate trace context over HTTP?

options.why: OAuth tokens are for authorization.
AMQP is a messaging protocol.
CloudEvents is an event schema.
Correct. The traceparent header carries the trace and parent span IDs.

questions.hint: Trace context travels in a header defined by a web standards body.
questions.explain: traceparent: version-traceId-parentSpanId-flags.

questions.q: In Application Insights, which field corresponds to the OpenTelemetry trace ID?

options.why: customDimensions holds span attributes.
cloud_RoleName identifies the service.
Correct. operation_Id links all telemetry in one distributed trace.
itemCount relates to sampling counts, not trace identity.

questions.hint: Application Insights uses its own name for the ID that ties a whole request together.
questions.explain: Join tables on operation_Id to follow one request.

questions.q: Given `traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01`, what is `00f067aa0ba902b7`?

options.text: The trace ID for the request
options.why: The trace ID is the 32-character second field.
Flags are the last field (01 = sampled).
Version is the first field (00).
Correct. The third field is the 16-hex-character parent span ID.

questions.hint: The header has four parts. Count which part this is.
questions.explain: The receiver creates a span with the same trace ID and this span as parent.

questions.q: Match each OpenTelemetry span kind to the Application Insights table it lands in.

items.why: Processing a queued message maps to requests.

questions.hint: Server spans become requests. Client and internal spans become dependencies.
questions.explain: SERVER and CONSUMER → requests; CLIENT, INTERNAL, PRODUCER → dependencies.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A team instruments a RAG pipeline with OpenTelemetry and exports to Application Insights.

rows.text: Switching to a different OpenTelemetry-compatible backend would require re-instrumenting the code.
rows.why: Instrument once; change exporters, not instrumentation.

rows.text: The trace ID in a traceparent header is 16 hexadecimal characters.
rows.why: The trace ID is 32 hex characters; the parent span ID is 16.

rows.text: Attributes set with span.set_attribute() appear in customDimensions.
Without context propagation, each service creates its own independent trace.
rows.why: Propagation is what links spans across services.

questions.hint: Think about context propagation, span identity, and where custom attributes end up.
questions.explain: Vendor-neutral instrumentation plus W3C propagation yields one correlated trace.

questions.q: An HTTP framework instrumentation library records incoming requests without any code from you. Which OpenTelemetry component sends that telemetry on to Application Insights?

options.why: Instrumentation libraries capture telemetry from frameworks. Exporters transmit it.
Propagation carries trace IDs between services. It doesn't send data to a backend.
The API defines the interfaces for creating telemetry. It doesn't send data anywhere.
Correct. Exporters serialize and send collected telemetry to a backend such as Azure Monitor.

questions.hint: OpenTelemetry has APIs, SDKs, instrumentation libraries, and one more part that ships data out.
questions.explain: OpenTelemetry components: APIs (interfaces), SDKs (processing, batching, sampling), instrumentation libraries (automatic capture), and exporters (send telemetry to backends). The Azure Monitor Distro bundles them.

questions.q: Which call initializes OpenTelemetry tracing, metrics and logging to Application Insights in a Python app?

options.why: That sets a span attribute.
That configures standard logging only.
get_tracer gets a tracer after configuration.
Correct. Call it once at startup to configure all three providers.

questions.hint: The Azure Monitor Distro has one function that sets everything up.
questions.explain: pip install azure-monitor-opentelemetry, then configure_azure_monitor().

questions.q: Which environment variable should hold the Application Insights connection string in production?

options.why: Correct. The Distro picks it up automatically and keeps it out of source code.
That sets the service name.
That's the Functions runtime storage setting.
That chooses the sampler.

questions.hint: Production configuration shouldn't live in code. Which environment variable does the Distro read?
questions.explain: Environment variable is recommended; code-based configuration is least recommended.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A Flask app calls an embeddings API with the requests library and queries PostgreSQL with psycopg2, after configure_azure_monitor().

rows.text: Incoming Flask requests are captured as server spans automatically.
The embeddings API calls need hand-written spans to appear as dependencies.
rows.why: The requests instrumentation captures them as client spans.

rows.text: psycopg2 queries appear as dependency spans automatically.
Log lines from logging.getLogger() need a separate exporter to reach Application Insights.

questions.hint: The Distro instruments common libraries automatically. Think about requests and the web framework.
questions.explain: The Distro auto-collects common HTTP, web, database, Azure SDK and logging telemetry.

questions.q: Four RAG services send telemetry to one Application Insights resource but appear as one node on the Application Map. What should you set?

options.text: A separate connection string for each service
options.why: They can share a resource; the role name is what separates nodes.

options.text: A higher sampling ratio on every service
options.why: Sampling doesn't affect role names.

options.text: SpanKind.SERVER set on every single span
options.why: Span kind doesn't name services.
Correct. Cloud role name comes from service.namespace + service.name.

questions.hint: Each service needs its own cloud role name, which comes from resource attributes.
questions.explain: For example rag-pipeline.embedding-service, rag-pipeline.llm-orchestrator.

questions.q: APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING points to the production resource, but code also passes a connection string for a test resource. Where does telemetry go?

options.text: Neither, because the conflict disables export
options.why: Conflicts don't disable export.

options.text: The test resource, because code takes priority
options.why: Correct. For the connection string, code has the highest priority.
The exporter sends to one connection string.

options.text: The production resource, because environment variables win
options.why: That precedence applies to sampling settings, not the connection string.

questions.hint: When code and environment disagree about the connection string, one of them wins.
questions.explain: Connection string precedence: code first, then environment variable.

questions.q: You can't change the embedding service's code, but it must appear on the Application Map as rag-pipeline.embedding-service. How can you set this?

options.text: Rename the container image to embedding-service
options.why: The image name doesn't set OpenTelemetry resource attributes.
Correct. Resource attributes can be set through environment variables, and the cloud role name is namespace.name.

options.text: Create a second Application Insights resource for the service
options.why: Separate resources don't set the role name, and they split the Application Map.
That isn't a variable the Distro reads for the role name.

questions.hint: Cloud role name comes from two OpenTelemetry resource attributes, which have standard environment variables.
questions.explain: The cloud role name is service.namespace + service.name. Set them in code (Resource.create) or with OTEL_SERVICE_NAME and OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES.

questions.q: A Flask RAG service uses psycopg2 for PostgreSQL. After you add the Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry Distro, where do the database queries appear?

options.text: As log records in the traces table
options.why: Queries are captured as spans, not as log records.

options.text: They don't appear unless you write a custom span for each query
options.why: psycopg2 is one of the libraries the Distro instruments automatically.

options.text: As dependency spans, with the database name and execution time
options.why: Correct. The Distro's psycopg2 instrumentation records queries as dependencies.

options.text: As request spans, because they run inside a request
options.why: Requests are incoming HTTP calls. Outgoing database calls are dependencies.

questions.hint: Outgoing calls from your service, including database calls, all land in one table.
questions.explain: The Distro instruments requests, urllib/urllib3, Flask/Django/FastAPI, psycopg2 and Azure SDK calls. Outgoing calls such as database queries become dependency spans.

questions.q: If you don't specify a kind when starting a span, which SpanKind is used?

options.why: Correct. INTERNAL is the default and maps to dependencies.
SERVER represents incoming requests.
CLIENT represents outgoing calls.
CONSUMER represents processing async messages.

questions.hint: Without a kind, OpenTelemetry assumes the span is work inside the service, not a call in or out.
questions.explain: Set kind explicitly for outgoing calls (CLIENT) or message processing (CONSUMER).

questions.q: You want to record which model and how many tokens each LLM call used, so you can filter traces later. What should you add?

options.why: Attributes keep the data on the span for querying.
Correct. Span attributes describe a specific operation and land in customDimensions.

options.text: A new tracer for each request
options.why: One tracer per component is enough.
Resource attributes describe the whole service.

questions.hint: Custom key-value context on a span is searchable later.
questions.explain: Use namespaced keys for searchability.

questions.q: A span named CallLlmApi represents an outgoing HTTP call to Azure OpenAI. Which kind should it use?

options.why: Correct. Outgoing calls are CLIENT spans (dependencies).
INTERNAL is for operations that don't cross process boundaries.
SERVER is for incoming requests.
CONSUMER is for processing async messages.

questions.hint: The span represents an outgoing call to another service.
questions.explain: Correct span kinds put telemetry in the right tables.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. Code inside `with tracer.start_as_current_span("GenerateEmbedding") as span:` catches a timeout exception and returns a fallback.

rows.text: The SDK still records the exception automatically.
rows.why: Only exceptions that propagate out are recorded automatically.

rows.text: Calling span.record_exception() and span.set_status() marks the span as failed with details.
rows.why: Do this when you handle the exception yourself.

rows.text: A span started inside this block becomes its child automatically.
rows.why: The SDK tracks the current span via context variables.

rows.text: The span must be ended manually with span.end().
rows.why: The context manager ends it when the block exits.

questions.hint: A caught exception is invisible to the SDK unless you record it. Child spans nest by themselves, and the with block ends the span.
questions.explain: start_as_current_span handles lifetime and parentage; caught errors need explicit recording.

questions.q: A request handler creates nested spans for a RAG query. Put them in the order they start in the waterfall.
questions.hint: The parent starts first, then its children in the order the code runs.
questions.explain: Nested context managers create parent-child spans; the waterfall shows each step's share of the time.

questions.q: Code sets sampling_ratio=0.5, but OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER=microsoft.fixed_percentage and OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG=0.1 are set on the host. What sampling applies?

options.why: Code wins for the connection string, not sampling.

options.text: About 10%; env vars win for sampling
options.why: Correct. For sampling, environment variables win.
They don't add up.

options.text: No sampling, because the settings conflict
options.why: Conflicts don't disable sampling.

questions.hint: For sampling, environment variables take precedence over code.
questions.explain: Adjust sampling via environment variables without redeploying.

questions.q: In Application Insights, which table receives log records emitted through Python's logging module?

options.why: customMetrics holds custom metric values.
dependencies holds client, internal and producer spans.
Correct. Log records land in the traces table.
requests holds server and consumer spans.

questions.hint: Log records aren't requests or dependencies. Their table name sounds like another pillar of observability.
questions.explain: Despite its name, the traces table holds logs; spans go to requests and dependencies.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A high-volume service uses fixed-percentage sampling at 0.05.

rows.text: Custom metrics are also sampled at 5%.
Counts in the Performance and Failures panes become less precise at lower ratios.
rows.why: Fewer data points make adjusted counts less precise.

rows.text: If the network drops, telemetry is cached and retried for up to 48 hours.
rows.why: Offline storage with retries is built in.

rows.text: Without any sampler configured, the Python Distro sends 100% of traces.

questions.hint: Sampling applies to traces, not custom metrics. Lower ratios make counts less precise. Think about offline caching and the default.
questions.explain: Sample traces for cost; metrics stay complete; offline storage covers outages.

questions.q: In the traceparent header 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01, what does the final 01 mean?

options.why: The version is the first field, 00.
Correct. The trace flags field 01 indicates the trace is sampled.
Retries aren't recorded in traceparent.

options.text: It's the first span in the trace
options.why: Span position isn't encoded in the header.

questions.hint: The four fields are version, trace ID, parent span ID, and one set of flags.
questions.explain: traceparent fields: version (00), 32-hex trace ID, 16-hex parent span ID, and trace flags (01 = sampled).

questions.q: Which KQL query links slow requests to the dependency calls inside the same distributed trace?

options.text: requests | union dependencies | order by duration desc
options.why: union stacks rows; it doesn't relate them by trace.

options.text: requests | where duration > 5000 | join kind=inner (dependencies) on cloud_RoleName
options.why: cloud_RoleName joins by service, not by trace.

options.text: requests | where duration > 5000 | join kind=inner (dependencies) on operation_Id
options.why: Correct. operation_Id identifies the trace shared by all its spans.
This summarizes dependencies without linking them to requests.

questions.hint: Requests and dependencies are joined on the field that identifies the whole operation.
questions.explain: operation_Id corresponds to the OpenTelemetry trace ID.

questions.q: Vector search spans are usually 100 ms but sometimes 5 s, mostly right after quiet periods, with normal result counts. What pattern does this suggest?

options.why: These are search spans, not embedding spans.
Correct. Slow clusters after inactivity, with normal search.result_count, point to cold starts.
Overflow appears on prompt assembly or LLM errors.
Rate limiting shows 429s on LLM calls.

questions.hint: Slow only after idle periods, with normal results, suggests something warming up.
questions.explain: Attributes like search.result_count separate cold starts from genuinely heavy queries.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A team investigates slow RAG responses in Application Insights.

rows.text: The Application Map shows average response time and failure rate per service node.
rows.why: Nodes and edges show key metrics.

rows.text: Selecting a span in the transaction view shows its custom attributes.
rows.why: Span details include attributes and exceptions.

rows.text: Custom span attributes can be queried as regular table columns without customDimensions.
rows.why: They live in customDimensions; extract them with KQL.

questions.hint: Look at the waterfall, the dependency durations, and whether attributes explain the slow spans.
questions.explain: Map → waterfall → KQL is the usual drill-down.
